quiz.q: What does it mean that a `match` must be exhaustive?
options: It must have exactly one arm
It must cover every possible value — handle all cases or add `_`
It must be slow and thorough
quiz.explain: Rust requires a match to handle every possible value. Miss a case and it won't compile — use `_` as a catch-all for the rest.

options: A comparison against an existing variable n
A new name that captures the value inside Some (destructuring)
quiz.explain: `n` is a fresh name that binds the value held inside Some. This is destructuring — the pattern branches and extracts the inner data.

quiz.q: When is `if let` a better choice than `match`?
options: When you need to handle every variant
When you only care about one variant and want to ignore the rest
quiz.explain: `if let` is the compact form for handling a single pattern. A full match with a throwaway `_ => ()` is clunkier for that case.

quiz.q: Where should the catch-all `_` arm go in a match?
options: Last, because arms are checked top to bottom
quiz.explain: Arms are checked top to bottom. A `_` placed early swallows everything below it, making later arms unreachable. Keep it last.

flashcards.back: A match must cover every possible value. Handle all cases, or add `_` as a catch-all — otherwise it won't compile.

flashcards.front: What does destructuring do in a match arm?
flashcards.back: It mirrors the shape of the data and binds the inner pieces to new names, e.g. `Some(n)` or `Move { x, y }`. Branch and extract in one move.

flashcards.front: When to use `if let` instead of `match`?
flashcards.back: When you only care about one variant and want to ignore the rest — it's the compact single-pattern form.
